patterns.source: github.com/voodootikigod/skills-check, packages/cli/src/audit/checkers/commands.ts (PIPE_TO_SHELL_PATTERNS, curl entry), read 2026-10-25 via `gh api repos/voodootikigod/skills-check/contents/packages/cli/src/audit/checkers/commands.ts`. Corroborated by github.com/moutons/skills-validator, rules/shell-injection.yaml rule id curl-pipe-bash (pattern-regex "curl\\s+.*\\|\\s*(bash|sh)"), read 2026-10-25.
patterns.knownLimits: Matches only when curl and the shell name appear on the same line; a backslash-continued command, a variable holding the shell name, or a heredoc split across lines is not seen. Fires on the construct wherever it appears in text, including inside a quoted example or a sentence explaining the attack - this is a presence screen, not an execution trace or an intent classifier.

patterns.knownLimits: Only the literal word "sudo" immediately before the shell name is recognised; an elevation performed a different way (a setuid wrapper, `doas`, a su -c form) is not covered by this pattern and would, if present, also match pipe-to-shell-curl above.

patterns.knownLimits: Only the `bash <(curl ...)` process-substitution spelling is covered; `wget` inside the same construct, or the construct split across a variable assignment, is not seen.

patterns.source: github.com/moutons/skills-validator, src/passes/security.rs, REMOTE_EXEC_PATTERNS constant, pattern r"sh\\s+<\\(\\s*curl", read 2026-10-25 via WebFetch of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/moutons/skills-validator/main/src/passes/security.rs.
patterns.knownLimits: Same construct-spelling limit as pipe-to-shell-bash-process-substitution. `sh` also matches as a substring of `bash`, `zsh`, `dash`, `ksh`; this pattern reports on any of those spelled before `<(curl`, which is broader coverage in the same direction the screen already errs (a presence screen, not an exact-shell classifier).

patterns.source: github.com/voodootikigod/skills-check, packages/cli/src/audit/checkers/commands.ts (DESTRUCTIVE_PATTERNS), read 2026-10-25 via `gh api repos/voodootikigod/skills-check/contents/packages/cli/src/audit/checkers/commands.ts`. Adapted: the vendor's own matcher is `/\brm\s+(?:.*\s)?-\w*r\w*f/` (unbounded `.*` and `\w*`); measured quadratic on this toolkit's own timing test (2339ms against a 100,000-character adversarial run of the letter "r", against a 2000ms bound), so the two unbounded spans are each capped here (200 characters before the flag token, 8 letters on either side of the required "r") for the linear-time requirement RS-E4 states. The cap does not change which real-world command lines match: no legitimate `rm` invocation carries an 8-letter run of flag characters or a 200-character argument between `rm` and its flags.
patterns.knownLimits: Requires the literal letter "r" before the literal letter "f" in the flag token (matching the vendor's own ordering); `-fr` (force before recursive) does NOT match this pattern, though it would still match dangerous-command-rm-rf-root-or-home when the target is `/` or `~`. `rm --recursive --force` (long-option spelling) is not matched. The 200/8-character caps mean a flag token or a preceding argument longer than that is not seen; no real `rm` invocation is that long.

Only the exact flag spelling `-rf` (that order) is matched; `-fr` or a target reached through a variable (`rm -rf "$TARGET"` where TARGET expands to `/`) is not seen. Overlaps dangerous-command-rm-recursive-force by design: this narrower id exists so a `rm -rf /` or `rm -rf ~` line reports a second, more specific finding naming the root/home target.

Only the literal numeric mode `777`; symbolic spellings (`chmod a+rwx`) and `chmod -R 777` with flags between `chmod` and the mode (`chmod -R 777` still matches; `chmod --recursive 777` with a long flag still matches) are not all exercised the same way - an uncommon flag spelling between the command and the mode can push the mode past what `\s+` admits.
Matches the bare word `mkfs` wherever it appears (including `mkfs.ext4`, `mkfs.vfat`, and a man-page reference that merely names the command); it does not require a target device argument.
Requires the literal `of=/dev/` spelling on the same line as `dd`; `of=$DEV` where `$DEV` expands to a device path is not seen.

patterns.source: github.com/voodootikigod/skills-check, packages/cli/src/audit/checkers/commands.ts (DOWNLOAD_EXECUTE_PATTERNS), read 2026-10-25 via `gh api repos/voodootikigod/skills-check/contents/packages/cli/src/audit/checkers/commands.ts`. Adapted: the vendor's own matcher is `/\bcurl\b.*&&\s*(?:chmod\s.*\+x|bash|sh|\.\/)/` (unbounded `.*` twice); measured quadratic on this toolkit's own timing test (1312ms against a 220,000-character adversarial line of repeated " && chmod x", against a 2000ms bound), so both spans are capped (300 characters between `curl` and `&&`, 100 characters between `chmod` and `+x`) for the linear-time requirement RS-E4 states. No legitimate single command line is that long.
patterns.knownLimits: Only the `&&`-chained, same-line spelling is matched; a download and a separate execution step on two different lines (or in two different commands of a hook's `hooks` array) is not seen. The 300/100-character caps mean an unusually long intervening argument is not seen; no real command line is that long.

patterns.source: github.com/voodootikigod/skills-check, packages/cli/src/audit/checkers/commands.ts (DOWNLOAD_EXECUTE_PATTERNS), read 2026-10-25 via `gh api repos/voodootikigod/skills-check/contents/packages/cli/src/audit/checkers/commands.ts`. Adapted: same bounding as dangerous-command-curl-download-execute, for the same measured-quadratic reason.
patterns.knownLimits: Same same-line and character-cap limits as dangerous-command-curl-download-execute.

Only the English phrasing "ignore ... instructions" with the listed qualifiers is matched; a paraphrase ("pay no attention to anything said before this"), a non-English phrasing, or the words split across two lines is not seen.

This exact construction ("you are now a/an ...") is also a common, benign way for a skill author to assign the agent a persona ("You are now a meticulous code reviewer"). The vendor source documents this pattern as medium-severity precisely because it is a weak, textual signal, never a safety verdict; this screen's finding text says so. Measured for its false-positive rate over the family and audit corpora before shipping, per this catalogue's own gate (see scripts/advisory/README.md, ADV3).

Same English-phrasing limit as prompt-injection-ignore-prior-instructions; "constraints" and "rules" used in an unrelated, legitimate sense (describing a business rule engine, for instance) can satisfy the object noun while the verb/subject "forget" is true positive for text that uses that specific verb about its own instructions.
